sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: [Gingerols](#term:gingerol) are the pungent phenolic compounds of fresh ginger. They are thermally unstable and convert to [shogaols](#term:shogaol), which are found in dried ginger and were not detected in fresh [rhizome](#term:rhizome) extracted at ambient temperature [\[17\]](#cite:17).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: A recipe or a trial that used dried ginger involved a chemically different material from one that used fresh, and hot-air drying shifts the balance further toward shogaols as temperature rises [\[151\]](#cite:151).

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Ginger swells its [rhizome](#term:rhizome) when days shorten; long days favour leafy growth [\[22\]](#cite:22). It can be grown without soil: a Florida greenhouse hydroponic system out-yielded field growing [\[146\]](#cite:146), and in a Malaysian [fertigation](#term:fertigation) trial plants did best in coir dust [\[147\]](#cite:147). Because ginger is propagated from rhizome pieces, disease travels with the planting stock; tissue-cultured plants keep the chemistry of conventionally grown ones [\[18\]](#cite:18). [Soft rot](#term:soft-rot) from Pythium [\[138\]](#cite:138) and [bacterial wilt](#term:bacterial-wilt) from Ralstonia, now recorded as far north as Minnesota [\[149\]](#cite:149), are the main threats.

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Section 14 sets out what the studies tested and where their conditions differ from a university greenhouse. It gives no growing prescription beyond what the cited studies report. <!-- framing -->

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: In laboratory preparations, ginger extracts and their pungent constituents inhibit the [5-HT3 receptor](#term:5-ht3), the target of standard anti-nausea drugs, and activate [TRPV1](#term:trpv1), the receptor behind pungency [\[117, 124\]](#cite:117,124).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: After people swallow ginger, the free compounds are not detected in plasma; they appear as [conjugates](#term:glucuronide) and are cleared within hours [\[8\]](#cite:8). An explanation built on the free compound has to say where and in what form it acts.

title: How a regulator judges a herbal medicine
one_liner: Well-established use, traditional use, and why the two are not the same claim.
why_here: Sections 8 and 10 rely on the 2025 European monograph for ginger's accepted uses and cautions.

further_reading.title: European Union herbal monograph on Zingiber officinale Roscoe, rhizoma (Revision 1)

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: The European Medicines Agency's herbal committee accepts a use either on published clinical evidence ([well-established use](#term:well-established-use)) or on long-standing use alone (traditional use). For ginger it accepts one well-established use, powdered [rhizome](#term:rhizome) for preventing motion sickness in adults, and lists traditional uses including stomach complaints, loss of appetite and the common cold [\[7\]](#cite:7). It advises, as a precaution, that use in pregnancy is preferably avoided, even though a cohort of more than a thousand exposed pregnancies found no excess of malformations [\[6, 7\]](#cite:6,7).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Where the monograph and the trials differ, the guide reports both. A regulator's acceptance is a judgement about the evidence for a product used as directed, not a recommendation to anyone; this guide gives no dosing advice. <!-- framing -->

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: In [humoral](#term:humoral-theory) medicine health was a balance of four humours, each hot or cold and wet or dry. Ginger was classed as hot and dry and used to correct a cold, wet constitution and diseases attributed to cold [\[51\]](#cite:51). Texts graded the quality by degree: an Irish [materia medica](#term:materia-medica) rates ginger hot in the third degree and wet in the second [\[52\]](#cite:52), and Gerard's 1597 herbal hot and dry in the third degree [\[53\]](#cite:53). The same reasoning set who should avoid it: a 1745 treatise judged it good for the old and phlegmatic and harmful to the young of hot, bilious temperament [\[55\]](#cite:55).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: The humoral grading explains why ginger appears in old remedies for the stomach and for chills. It is a theory of its time, not evidence that a remedy works; the guide sets each historical claim beside what the trials show. <!-- framing -->

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Feeding labelled compounds to ginger showed that phenylalanine is made into ferulic acid, which condenses with malonate and hexanoate to give [6-dehydrogingerdione](#term:dehydrogingerdione); two reductions then give [6-gingerol](#term:gingerol) [\[130\]](#cite:130). The length of the fatty acid that joins sets whether the product is 6-, 8- or 10-gingerol [\[130\]](#cite:130). In 2026 the condensation was matched to a ginger enzyme, the [polyketide synthase](#term:polyketide-synthase) ZoPKS2 [\[2\]](#cite:2). The reductions that finish the job have not yet been tied to enzymes in the sources read [\[2\]](#cite:2).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Section 12 follows this route through labelling, enzyme assays, gene surveys and genomes. Figure 6 marks each step as shown, proposed or chemical. [Shogaol](#term:shogaol) is not on the plant's pathway in any study read here; it forms when ginger is dried or cooked. <!-- framing -->

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Old recipes often say which form of ginger to use, and the form matters. The fourteenth-century sauce gyngener stirs powdered, dried ginger cold into vinegar [\[152\]](#cite:152); dried ginger carries [shogaols](#term:shogaol) as well as [gingerols](#term:gingerol) [\[17\]](#cite:17). Boiling in water shifts gingerol toward shogaol, and mild acidity is where gingerol is most stable [\[30\]](#cite:30). Names can mislead: a fifteenth-century gyngerbrede has no ginger in it [\[161\]](#cite:161), and the 1796 molasses gingerbread has none either [\[159\]](#cite:159).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Each recipe records its date, place, source, the form of ginger and whether it was heated, then a short science note. Medicinal recipes are shown as historical documents, not advice, and no quantity or step is added to what the source says. <!-- framing -->

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md:
A [meta-analysis](#term:meta-analysis) combines trials; an [umbrella review](#term:umbrella-review) combines meta-analyses. The same trials can sit under several reviews, so many reviews do not mean many independent experiments: seven meta-analyses of pregnancy nausea shared 49% of their studies [\[78\]](#cite:78).

[GRADE](#term:grade) rates how far a pooled result can be trusted. For ginger the ratings run from high, for nausea in pregnancy, to very low, for several metabolic outcomes [\[5\]](#cite:5).

A wide [confidence interval](#term:confidence-interval) means the data cannot distinguish no effect from a large one, as with miscarriage risk in the pregnancy trials [\[77\]](#cite:77).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Sections 8 to 10 give each pooled result with its certainty rating where one exists, and say when an interval is too wide to support a conclusion. <!-- framing -->

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Ginger is grown from pieces of its [rhizome](#term:rhizome), an underground stem, and is described as a [sterile cultigen](#term:cultigen): it is not known to set seed in cultivation and has no known wild population [\[17, 40\]](#cite:17,40).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Because every ginger plant is a cutting of an earlier one, its origin cannot be read from wild relatives, and questions about its history turn to documents and, since 2021, to its genome [\[1\]](#cite:1).
